query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount (≈0.1 at.%) of carbon to a refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) (e.g., Mo–Nb–Re–Ta–W based) will promote the in situ formation of stable carbide precipitates (such as Ta3C and Nb3C) during high-temperature operation, thereby enhancing high-temperature strength and creep resistance while leaving room-temperature ductility and the alloy’s density largely unaffected.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high-entropy alloy composed of refractory elements (e.g., Mo, Nb, Re, Ta, W) with a disordered solid solution phase and acceptable room-temperature mechanical performance but limited high-temperature strength.
generation.intervention: Addition of a trace level of carbon (around 0.1 at.%) into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature service conditions relevant to jet turbine applications (operating temperatures in the range of ~800–1000 °C under cyclic/tensile or creep loading), with corresponding room-temperature conditions for baseline performance assessment.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation of nano-scale carbide phases (e.g., Ta3C, Nb3C) during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The formation of fine, stable carbide precipitates at elevated temperatures provides a precipitation-strengthening effect by impeding dislocation motion. Because the trace carbon does not significantly alter the overall microstructure at room temperature, the alloy maintains its ductility and low density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped RHEA, the carbon-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures, while room-temperature tensile properties (ductility and strength) and density remain essentially unchanged.
generation.baseline: The mechanical performance and density of the undoped refractory HEA under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: This strengthening effect is expected to hold for alloys with similar compositions and processing histories under thermal exposures typical of jet turbine environments; the hypothesis may not apply if the carbon level is significantly different or if thermal cycles cause carbide coarsening/dissolution.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of high-temperature strength improvement is uncertain due to potential variations in carbide precipitate size, distribution, and long-term stability under jet turbine operating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with identical refractory HEA compositions (e.g., Mo–Nb–Re–Ta–W): one set without carbon and one with ≈0.1 at.% carbon. Process both samples identically. Conduct high-temperature tensile and creep tests within the jet turbine operational temperature range (~800–1000 °C) and perform room-temperature tensile tests. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify the formation, size, and distribution of carbide precipitates in the carbon-doped alloy.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and creep rate
Microstructural analysis (carbide precipitate identification and distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength or creep resistance compared to the undoped ones, or if room-temperature ductility and density are detrimentally affected, then the hypothesis is falsified. In addition, a lack of detectable carbide precipitates in the carbon-doped alloy under high-temperature conditions would also falsify the proposed mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
